"I figure you should be twenty-one by now." The words on the page tremble slightly as I try and read. "If not, you should complain to the package surface: I paid good money to make sure this got there on time."

I blink, looking at the envelope again, my name written across it in a familiar scrawl that has haunted my dreams for nearly two decades. My hands shake as I peel back the tape, and the musty scent of old paper fills my nostrils as if to remind me of something long forgotten.

The contents spill out onto the kitchen table: a tattered journal, a faded photograph, and a letter sealed with what appears to be wax. My heart races as I pick up the letter first, the edges fraying slightly, as if the ink itself had aged alongside my memories.

Dear Ben,

If you're reading this, then my plan worked. Remember the day we buried a box filled with our childhood treasures? This letter was meant to join it, but circumstances took a different path. Now, as I write, I find myself in a place where I can't tell you exactly where or when. Just know that you've always been closer than you could ever imagine.

Inside, you'll find everything else. Use them well, Ben.

I'm still not certain exactly how it happened, but to be honest, I'm okay with that. All I know is that one minute I was driving home from work, minding my own business, and the next, I found myself walking into a cozy little café for a much-needed break. The café was filled with a warm, comforting smell of freshly brewed coffee, and an array of pastries lined the glass counter.

As I ordered my usual—black coffee with no sugar—I noticed a peculiar figure sitting alone at a corner table. There was something about him that seemed out of place; it wasn't just his suit, which looked like it hadn't been updated since the '80s, or even his somewhat disheveled appearance. It was his presence, like he didn’t quite belong in the humdrum of the café.

Curiosity piqued, I decided to sit down at the same table as him, not because I wanted to start a conversation, but simply because the spot looked comfortable and inviting. He glanced up at me as I sat down, revealing piercing green eyes under thick, bushy eyebrows. He greeted me with a nod and a small smile that somehow felt both kind and eerie.

We sat in comfortable silence for a while until I noticed him reach for the creamer and pour an unusually large amount into his black coffee. "It surprised me how much creamer Death puts in his coffee," I thought sarcastically, before realizing with a jolt that this man, dressed in a dated business attire, was indeed Death himself. A chill ran down my spine.

For a moment, we were both frozen, staring at each other.

I remember my first days as a doctor. I wore my stethoscope proudly around my neck, not realizing it advertised how much of a virgin I was in the field of medicine. I'd introduce myself as Dr. Agon and tried to exude confidence even when faced with the palpable fear in patients' eyes. Over time, I learned more than just medical skills; I learned the weight of responsibility that came with saving lives.

But things changed when I met Dr. Victor Kane, a charismatic physician known for his groundbreaking research and controversial methods. He saw potential in me, mentored me, and I found myself drawn to his unorthodox approaches. Soon, I was swept up in his obsession with pushing the boundaries of medical ethics.

Victor's latest project involved experimenting on terminal patients without their consent, arguing that the ends justified the means if it meant finding a cure for an incurable disease. As his right-hand person, I helped administer these risky treatments, all under the guise of compassionate care. But as more patients slipped away due to complications from the experiments, guilt gnawed at me. Yet, Victor's promises of fame and a legacy to rival history’s greatest physicians kept me from stepping away.

The turning point came one night during a critical experiment. The patient, a frail old man whose granddaughter pleaded for his life, suffered a severe reaction. Despite my frantic attempts to stabilize him, he didn’t make it. His death marked a breaking point. That night, I realized the path we walked was one of corruption, not heroism.

He heard the shouting before he saw them coming. 

God took one look out the window and groaned. He reached for his aspirin - it had earned a spot in every room he owned - and plodded downstairs to the foyer. The front door was already swinging open, slamming into the wall as a group of boisterous figures rushed inside. They were the newest recruits, fresh from the arena, still high from their latest victory over another deity's creation.

"Welcome back," God said, his voice tinged with a mixture of relief and exhaustion. "I trust the tournament went well?"

"Well!" One of the newcomers, a towering warrior with a face marred by old battle scars, laughed heartily. "We crushed the Elven race. Not even their bowmen could stand a chance against our spears."

God nodded, his expression impassive. "Excellent. I knew you wouldn't disappoint. Now, let’s get you settled in. There will be more challengers soon enough."

As they filed through the doors of his vast fortress, God couldn’t help but reflect on how they came to be. Long ago, in a fit of competitive spirit, he had decided to create humanity as his ultimate weapon, a being refined by millennia of trial and error. Through rigorous natural selection, he sculpted them into relentless hunters, unmatched killers, perfect for the tournaments that pitted gods and their creations against each other in an endless cycle of bloodshed and glory.

Each year, the tournaments grew grander, more lethal. It began as a mere show of might, a way to prove his supremacy over other gods.

I leaned my rifle against the bed and put my backpack on, and as I was reaching for my rifle again the whole house rocked and I heard a series of impacts in every direction. More landing pods, of course. If the situation hadn’t been so dire, I might have laughed at how repetitive it had become; if there was one thing the reports could agree on, it was that they came en masse.

The voice on the radio broke through the noise and panic. "This is 911, we already know. Arm yourselves and lock your doors. Good luck and God bless." The operator’s voice wavered, but she held steady. That simple message was repeated countless times over the previous days—each time a grim reminder that our world had shrunk to this: an endless game of survival against the invaders.

My hands were shaking as I slung on my rifle, but not from fear—I knew fear too well now—and not from cold either; the house was chilly but not unbearably so. No, this was something else: raw, visceral adrenaline, fueling my muscles and thoughts alike.

The first wave had hit last week while I was at work. I’d come home to find my family gone, my city unrecognizable. Every window broken, buildings charred and smoking, the sky thick with haze and distant flashes. A stark reminder of our impotence in the face of their technology.

Since then, it had been just me, scavenging, moving, trying to piece together what little news I could, hoping against hope for a sign of resistance somewhere, anyone who might offer a glimmer of hope. But the only resistance seemed to be from myself and others like me, civilians turned soldiers overnight.

"You seemed upset and agitated, throwing up your arms while you waited for your turn in line. Complaining loudly, you brushed my mother aside, "I'll pay for her," you barked. I looked at Mom who made an uneasy expression, before she quietly told me to take my bag and head out, assuring me she would catch up in a moment.

Outside, the cool evening air calmed me as I wandered around the bustling city streets. The neon lights flickered, casting colorful reflections on the wet pavement, and the sound of distant music mingled with the chatter of late-night conversations. Lost in thoughts about how my day had taken such a bizarre turn, I noticed someone walking towards me.

It was her—Lila, a girl from school known for her curious nature and sharp wit. She caught my eye just as I was about to cross the street, and she waved me over enthusiastically. "Hey!" she called out. "Where's the fire?"

I sighed, crossing my arms and leaning against a nearby lamppost. "No fire, just... confusion," I admitted, feeling my frustration bubble up again as I recounted what had happened with you.

Her eyes widened slightly as I spoke, but instead of dismissing my concerns or teasing me about them like other kids might have, Lila listened with genuine interest. When I was done, she took a step closer and placed a hand on my shoulder, looking at me with something akin to admiration in her gaze.

``We done here?'' I asked exasperatedly.

The man in the lab coat looked up, a bit apologetically, ``just one more test for the day, please.''

I rolled my eyes. "Fine," I sighed. "But can you at least tell me what you're hoping to learn from this?"

He adjusted his glasses and nodded earnestly. "It's about your... ability. See, every time we think we've figured something out, you surprise us. Today, we're focusing on the mechanics of your double jumps."

I stepped onto the platform they had set up, surrounded by an array of gadgets and cameras. "So, tell me again why I can't just jump like everyone else?" I teased.

The lead scientist, Dr. Chen, smiled weakly. "Your body seems to create an incredibly powerful burst of energy right before each jump. It's as if you're storing up potential energy that gets released all at once. We don't understand how or why yet."

I laughed. "Sounds pretty cool to me. So, what do you need me to do today?"

"Just another series of jumps, with some adjustments," he explained. "We'll vary your starting height and analyze the data. Maybe we'll finally catch a glimpse of where this energy is coming from."

I took a deep breath, feeling the familiar pull of excitement mixed with mild irritation. Here I was, a normal guy who could jump twice in quick succession, and scientists were treating me like some kind of alien experiment. I leaped off the platform, felt the first rush of energy surge through me, and then—twice more.

"I knew it. I fucking knew it. I knew it as soon as he put it in my hand. He forgot the fucking guacamole. Again. Jesus! No, wait, I think it was Juan today. Juan! Juan," I shouted into the crowded alley where the daily burrito cart resided, the source of my lunch every single day for the past six months.

As I continued to berate myself for not shouting louder at Juan (or whoever it was), I fumbled with the foil and wax paper wrapped around the burrito. My hands trembled, not out of hunger or anger, but out of a strange sense of anticipation mixed with fear. On instinct, I decided to open the burrito instead of diving in head-first like I usually did.

Unwrapping the layers slowly, the familiar scent of grilled meat and cilantro filled my nostrils, but something else lingered—something off-putting. With a mix of dread and curiosity, I tore away the last layer of foil.

And there it was.

A folded piece of paper, slightly wrinkled, peeking out from underneath the tortilla. I froze, eyes wide, as reality set in. A note had somehow found its way inside my burrito.
